title: Masonry Scope Gaps: Penetrations, Sleeves, and Firestopping in Division 04
summary: Scope Agent flagged masonry packages on 95% of projects reviewed. Here's what GC estimators miss in Division 04 before bid day.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Provision's Scope Gap Index flagged at least one gap in 21 of 22 masonry packages reviewed in Q3 2026, across 20 projects from 16 general contractors.
- Penetrations, sleeves, and firestopping were the most-flagged job: 91% of Division 04 packages had at least one flag here.
- Masonry flags are overwhelmingly inferred, meaning the work is required by the drawings but nobody's scope names who does it.
- Scaffolding, anchors, and sealants each appeared in more than 85% of packages. These are not edge cases.
- Closing these gaps before bid day takes one sentence per item in the scope. It does not take a redesign.


Masonry bids look simple. One sub. One wall. One trade. That framing is exactly why Division 04 scope packages bleed change orders.


The mason describes the wall. The wall doesn't describe who sleeves the duct through it, who anchors the lintel, or who patches the opening after the electrical sub cuts in late. Those jobs sit between trades, or they sit in nobody's scope at all. They show up on a change order after the wall is up.


Provision's[Scope Gap Index](https://provision.com/scope-gap-index) for Q3 2026 tracked 22 Division 04 packages across 20 projects from 16 general contractors. Twenty-one of 22 had at least one flag from[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) . Nine jobs were flagged in more than three-quarters of all packages. Penetrations led at 91%.


This post covers what those flags point at, why they keep appearing, and how to close them in the scope before bid day.


## Why Masonry Scope Gaps Are Different From Other Trades


Most trades have shared-work problems. MEP trades fight over the trench. Drywall and millwork fight over blocking. Masonry is different in one important way: its gaps are almost entirely inferred, not coordination failures.


Of the 676 flags Scope Agent raised across all 22 masonry packages, 556 were inferred flags and 120 were coordination flags. That is more than four in five pointing at work the documents require and nobody's scope names. Not a hand-off problem. A gap in coverage.


The mason scopes the wall. Full stop. Everything that happens around the wall, through the wall, or on top of the wall is assumed to belong to someone else. Often, it does not belong to anyone.


As one Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC put it: "If you miss anything, they'll bill it." That quote is about subcontractor behavior broadly, but it describes masonry precisely. Subs have become more deliberate about naming what they exclude. When you don't name it in the scope, it becomes a question on bid day or a change order later.


## The Nine Jobs Flagged in More Than 75% of Masonry Packages


Every one of these appeared in 17 or more of the 22 packages Scope Agent reviewed. They are ranked by share flagged.

Source:[Provision Scope Gap Index, Q3 2026](https://provision.com/scope-gap-index) . 22 Division 04 packages, 20 projects, 16 general contractors. A flag is Scope Agent's judgment that a job is needed and nobody's scope names it, or that it sits between two trades. It is not a confirmed omission on any single project.


## Penetrations, Sleeves, and Firestopping: The Gap That Leads Every Masonry Bid


This job topped the masonry ranking at 91%, with 20 inferred flags and 6 coordination flags across 20 of 22 packages. It is the most consistent masonry gap in the Index.


The pattern is straightforward. The mason builds the wall. The mechanical sub runs duct through it. The plumbing sub runs pipe through it. Neither sub built in a sleeve. The electrical sub needs a conduit run through the rated wall and nobody cored it. The fire inspector arrives and the penetrations are bare.


### What the Scope Needs to Say


Three questions settle this in the package:


1. Who supplies the sleeves? Each trade typically supplies sleeves for their own systems. That needs to be in writing.
2. Who builds them in? The mason should build in sleeves supplied by MEP trades before the wall goes up. If the wall is already up, coring costs more and someone pays for it.
3. Who firestops? In a rated wall, every penetration needs a listed firestopping assembly. The mason's scope rarely includes it. The mechanical sub's scope often excludes it too. That is the gap.


Require a combined penetration drawing before the wall starts. Name who firestops each assembly type. One sentence each. That is all it takes.


For a broader view of how inferred scope language creates financial exposure, the[Scope Gap Playbook chapter on trade-specific scope gaps](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) covers the mechanics behind these patterns, including why $300K in lead-lined glass for a hospital imaging suite ended up absorbed by the GC under "readily inferable" language.


## Anchors, Embeds, and Connections: The Coordination Gap


Anchors appeared in 19 of 22 masonry packages, with 19 inferred flags and 13 coordination flags. The coordination count matters here. This is not just missing coverage. It is a genuine hand-off between trades.


The steel sub needs a wall tie anchor cast into the mason's backup wythe. The structural engineer's drawings show the embed. The mason's scope does not name it. The steel sub assumes the mason provides it. The mason assumes it comes with the steel package. On bid day, both subs price the wall without the anchor. After award, someone gets a change order.


### How to Close It


- Put the anchor and embed schedule in the masonry scope. Reference the structural drawings by sheet number.
- Name who supplies each item and who sets it. Supply and installation are separate responsibilities.
- Include relieving angles for multi-story brick veneer. These sit at every floor line and they appear in the structural drawings, not the masonry spec.


An Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC described the shift in how subs handle these gaps: "We have less subs who just kind of a gentleman's agreement. They've become more quick to clarify that we're not including that one piece of scope." Anchors are exactly the kind of item that used to be a handshake and is now a RFI.


## Sealants, Flashing, and Waterproofing: Where the Roofer and the Mason Both Stop


Sealants were flagged in 19 of 22 packages. Eighteen of those were inferred flags and 10 were coordination flags. This is a joint-ownership problem.


The mason installs through-wall flashing. The roofer installs base flashing at the parapet. The waterproofing sub handles the foundation. Where one stops and another starts, somebody has to seal the line. The drawings show the joint. No scope names who owns it.


Control joint sealant is the most common inferred gap here. The masonry spec describes the joint layout. It does not always name who fills the joint or who backs it. Sealant at the masonry-to-window-frame interface is another. The glazing sub stops at the frame. The mason stops at the opening. The joint is in neither scope.


### The Fix


State whether the mason installs flashing supplied by the waterproofing sub, or the reverse. Name who seals control joints and what backer rod specification applies. Add a single line about the masonry-to-storefront interface. These are not long clauses. They are one sentence each.


## Scaffolding: The Gap Nobody Thinks They Have


Scaffolding was flagged in 18 of 22 masonry packages. All 18 were inferred flags. Not a single one was a coordination flag.


That is the finding. Masonry is the scaffolding trade. And Scope Agent still found 18 of 22 packages silent on who supplies it, who erects it, who gets it engineered above the threshold height, and whether the siding sub gets to use it after the mason is done.


When the siding sub finds scaffold already on site, they price against it. If the mason's scope didn't include the siding sub's access duration, the mason submits a change order for extended scaffold rental. This is a small-dollar item that generates a disproportionate amount of bid-day confusion.


Name the trade. Name the duration. Say which other trades may use it and under what conditions. Four lines in the masonry scope closes this entirely.


## Openings: The One Place Masonry Flags Point at Another Trade


Openings, cutting and patching drew 17 flags, with 14 of those as coordination flags. That is the highest coordination count in the Division 04 ranking. It points at a hand-off problem, not a coverage gap.


The mason builds the opening. The hollow-metal door frame arrives late from the door sub. The electrical sub cuts a box through the block after the wall is up. The HVAC sub needs a louvre that wasn't on the drawings at bid. Someone patches the block afterward. Nobody priced it.


### How to Write It


Decide in the scope whether the mason builds every opening shown on bid-day drawings, or whether they only build what is dimensioned and detailed at the time of their award. Addenda happen. Drawings change. If the scope does not address late-breaking openings, every one of them is a change order.


Name who patches openings cut by other trades. One sentence. It prevents an argument that runs for weeks after substantial completion.


## The Anti-Patterns That Create These Gaps


The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) , built from 200-plus GC interviews, names the habits that produce these patterns. Several apply directly to masonry:


- **"As per plans and specs."** This is the most-cited anti-pattern in the playbook. It is especially dangerous in masonry because the drawings show the wall and the spec describes the material. Neither document names the jobs around the wall.
- **Copy-paste from a previous similar job.** A masonry scope from a tilt-up warehouse does not cover a CMU core wall in a hospital. The firestopping requirements alone are different.
- **Junior estimators stuffing previous scopes verbatim.** The scope gets longer. It does not get more accurate. Items that were not in the previous job do not appear. Items the last sub specifically excluded still appear.
- **The five-minutes-before-bid review.** Masonry scopes reviewed in the final hour before close do not get the penetration drawing checked. They get a price check.


The fix is Habit 1 from the playbook: drawings-first, not boilerplate-first. Pull the mechanical and plumbing drawings before you open the masonry scope template. The penetrations are already on the drawings. The scope just has to name who owns them.


## What This Costs When You Miss It


Penetration and firestopping gaps are not five-figure items on most projects. But they compound. A hospital with 400 rated-wall penetrations across four masonry packages, each missing firestopping coverage, becomes a six-figure negotiation after the walls are up. The GC absorbs it under "readily inferable" language or pays for it in a change order.


The Arcadis Global Construction Disputes Report puts the average North American construction dispute at $60.1 million. Errors and omissions in contract documents rank as the leading cause of those disputes in North America. Masonry scope gaps are a small part of a large pattern. They are also one of the easiest parts to close.


A 2018 PlanGrid and FMI study put U.S. rework costs from miscommunication and bad project data at $31.3 billion. Twenty-six percent of that rework was attributed to communication breakdowns. A masonry scope that does not say who firestops is a communication breakdown priced into the wall.


## How Scope Agent Flags These Gaps Before Bid Day


Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) reads the full project document set: drawings, specifications, and addenda together. It does not read the masonry spec in isolation. It reads it against the mechanical drawings that show penetrations, against the structural drawings that show embeds, and against the fire-protection spec that names the assembly ratings.


When it generates a Division 04 scope package, it flags items as inferred (the job is required but nobody's scope names who does it) or coordination (the job sits between two trades). Your estimator reviews the flags and decides which ones are real on this project.


Across the 22 masonry packages in the Q3 2026 Index, Scope Agent raised 676 flags. It did that at 97.01% match accuracy on scope item extraction across its internal validation dataset. The human estimator baseline on the same exercise was 91.3%, at roughly four days per project.


The goal is not to replace the estimator's judgment. It is to make sure the judgment happens on the full list, not the list that survived a Friday afternoon scope review.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What are the most common masonry scope gaps in Division 04?


Penetrations, sleeves, and firestopping top the list. Provision's Scope Gap Index flagged this job in 91% of 22 masonry packages reviewed in Q3 2026. Anchors and embeds, sealants and flashing, scaffolding, and openings each appeared in more than 80% of packages.


### Who is responsible for firestopping in a CMU wall?


The masonry spec rarely assigns firestopping. The mechanical and plumbing specs often exclude it too. That gap is the problem. The GC needs to name the responsible trade in the scope, reference the rated-wall assembly, and require a combined penetration drawing before the wall starts.


### Why does scaffolding keep appearing as a masonry scope gap?


The mason is the scaffolding trade, so estimators assume it is covered. Provision's Scope Gap Index found scaffolding flagged in 18 of 22 masonry packages, all as inferred gaps. Supply, erection, engineering above threshold height, and access for other trades are rarely written into the scope.


### What does "inferred" mean in a masonry scope flag?


An inferred flag means Scope Agent judged that a job is required by the drawings or specifications, but no scope document names who performs it. It is not a confirmed omission on that specific project. Your estimator reviews the flag and decides whether it applies.


### How do I write a masonry scope that covers penetrations correctly?


Name who supplies sleeves for each system (typically each MEP trade for their own), require the mason to build in sleeves before the wall goes up, and name who firestops each rated-wall penetration type. Require a combined penetration drawing before wall construction begins. Three sentences closes the most common gap.


### What is the Division 04 scope gap rate from the Provision Scope Gap Index?


In Q3 2026, Scope Agent flagged at least one scope gap in 21 of 22 masonry packages reviewed across 20 projects from 16 general contractors. That is a 95% flag rate for the division. Nine individual jobs were flagged in more than 75% of packages.


### How does the Scope Gap Playbook apply to masonry bids?


The Scope Gap Playbook, built from 200-plus GC interviews, identifies "as per plans and specs" as the leading anti-pattern in trade scope writing. It applies directly to masonry: the drawings show the wall, but they do not name who owns the work around it. The playbook's drawings-first habit closes this before bid day.
